title: 論語 為政第二
source: Confucius 孔子 and his disciples, 論語 (the Analects), book 2, 〈為政〉, in the received text as printed in Zhu Xi 朱熹, 論語集注 (part of his 四書章句集注, completed c. 1190), from the Wenyuange 文淵閣 copy of the Siku Quanshu 四庫全書 (1782), as transcribed by the Kanseki Repository (Kanripo, KR1h0015). Collated character by character against two further pre-1930 printings, both transcribed by Kanripo: Ruan Yuan's 1816 Nanchang reprint of the Song edition of 論語注疏 (KR1h0004) and He Yan's 論語集解 in the Sibu Congkan photographic reprint of a Song edition (KR1h0005). Readings that change the sense are noted in the notes; graphic variants (悌 for 弟, 爲 for 為) are not. Zhu Xi's text is substantially the one James Legge printed in The Chinese Classics, vol. 1 (Hong Kong, 1861), and the passage numbering is the standard one. All punctuation is editorial — the original has none. Characters are traditional, as the edition prints them (衆, not 眾). Translations are made fresh from the Chinese. Pronunciation convention: modern Mandarin, given in Hanyu Pinyin — an admitted anachronism, and the living convention for reading these texts. Any prepared audio is synthesized speech in that same modern Mandarin convention; the exact voice used is recorded in audio/<id>/voice.txt and is fixed for every Chinese text.
about: Book 2 of the Analects, 為政 Wéi zhèng, named, as every book is, from its first words ("Conducting government…"). The Analects is a collection of short sayings and exchanges of Confucius (Kǒngzǐ, 551–479 BC) and his disciples, put together by their followers over several generations; the twenty books were not composed as a whole, and nothing in them was written down by Confucius himself. This book begins and ends with government — ruling by virtue and the rites rather than by decree and punishment (2.1, 2.3, 2.19–2.21) — and between them come Confucius' account of his own life decade by decade (2.4), four different answers to the question 'what is filial devotion?' (2.5–2.8), and sayings on learning, knowing, and the gentleman. Each numbered passage (2.1–2.24, the standard numbering) begins a new card; longer passages are cut where Zhu Xi's commentary interrupts the text. The original has no punctuation: every comma, quotation mark and full stop is an editor's interpretation. Read the characters; the pinyin under each one is a reading aid you can hide with the transcription button.

sentences.t:
子曰：「
為政以德，
譬如北辰，
居其所而衆星共之。」

morph.gloss: the North Star — the pole of the sky

sentences.l:
The Master said: “Conducting government by virtue —
compare it to the North Star:
it dwells in its place, and the many stars face toward it.”
sentences.i: The Master said: “Govern by virtue, and you are like the North Star, which keeps still in its place while all the other stars face toward it.”
sentences.n: The book is named from its first two characters, 為政 'conducting government'. Zhu Xi plays on two old sound-glosses: 政 zhèng 'government' is 正 zhèng 'to set right', and 德 dé 'virtue' is 得 dé 'what one has gained' — the Way practised until it is one's own. 北辰 is the pole of the sky, the point the heavens turn round; Zhu Xi calls it 'the pivot of heaven'. 共 is read gǒng here, the word later written 拱, 'to turn toward, to face as in salute' (Zhu Xi: 共音拱…向也); the everyday reading gòng 'together' does not fit. The picture is of rule without effort: the ruler does not move, and everything orders itself around him.

sentences.t:
子曰：「《詩》三百，
一言以蔽之，
曰：『思無邪。』」
sentences.l:
The Master said: “The Odes, three hundred —
one phrase covers them:
it says, ‘In thought, nothing crooked.’”
sentences.i: The Master said: “The Odes number three hundred, and a single phrase sums them all up: ‘No crookedness in thought.’”
sentences.n: The Odes held 305 poems; 'three hundred' is the round number (Zhu Xi: 舉大數). 一言 is 'one phrase', not 'one word' — 言 is a saying, here three characters. 以蔽之 is 以 with its object left out, 'with (it) cover them': Zhu Xi glosses 蔽 as 蓋 'to cover, to sum up'. 思無邪 is a line from the ode 駉 (Odes 297), where it describes horses running straight. In the ode 思 may be only a filler particle; Confucius, and Zhu Xi after him, take it as 'thought', and so the line becomes a verdict on the whole collection: whether a poem shows good or bad, its use is to leave the reader's feelings set straight. 邪 is read xié 'crooked'; the reading yé is a question particle.

sentences.t:
子曰：「
道之以政，
齊之以刑，
民免而無恥。

morph.gloss: make even, bring to one standard

sentences.l:
The Master said: “Lead them by decrees,
make them even by punishments:
the people evade, and have no shame.
sentences.i: The Master said: “Lead the people with decrees and hold them to one standard with punishments, and they will slip clear of the penalties and feel no shame.
sentences.n: 道 is the verb dǎo 'to lead', later written 導 — He Yan's text writes 導 here, and Zhu Xi glosses 道猶引導. 之 after each verb is 'them', the people, who are named only in the third clause. Zhu Xi on the words: 政 here is laws and prohibitions, 齊 'to make one', to bring everyone to the same line. 免 is to get off: they avoid the penalty, but, he says, the wish to do wrong has not gone.

sentences.t:
道之以德，
齊之以禮，
有恥且格。」
sentences.l:
Lead them by virtue,
make them even by the rites:
they have shame, and moreover reach the good.”
sentences.i: Lead them with virtue and hold them to one standard with the rites, and they will have a sense of shame, and will come to the good as well.”
sentences.n: The second half answers the first word for word, changing only the means — 德 for 政, 禮 for 刑 — and the result. 且 'and moreover' adds a second result to the first. 格 is the hard word. Zhu Xi glosses it 至 'to arrive', 'reach the good', and records a second reading, 正 'to correct (themselves)'. Zhu Xi adds that government and punishment are not to be thrown away, but they are tools; virtue and the rites are the root.

sentences.t:
子曰：「
吾十有五而志于學，
sentences.l: The Master said: “I, at ten and five, set my intent on learning;
sentences.i: The Master said: “At fifteen my intent was fixed on learning;
sentences.n: This passage is Confucius' account of his own life, one stage to a decade. 十有五 'ten and five' is the old way of writing fifteen: 有 between the tens and the units is read yòu, 'and moreover' (later 又). 而 here simply joins the age to what happened at it. 志 is where the heart is aimed. Zhu Xi notes that in antiquity a boy entered the 'greater learning' at fifteen, and takes 學 to be that learning — the way of the great school. He Yan's text reads 志乎學, the same sense.

sentences.t: 三十而立，
sentences.l: at thirty, established;
sentences.i: at thirty I was established in it;
sentences.n: Each stage is the same three-part line: an age, 而, a verb. 立 is 'to stand': Zhu Xi says he could stand by himself, holding firm to what he had learned, with no further need to fix his intent.

sentences.t: 四十而不惑，
sentences.l: at forty, not perplexed;
sentences.i: at forty I was no longer misled;
sentences.n: 惑 is to be confused, led astray. Zhu Xi: nothing in the world's affairs left him in doubt — he knew clearly, and no longer had to hold on by effort.

sentences.t: 五十而知天命，
sentences.l: at fifty, knew the decree of Heaven;
sentences.i: at fifty I knew what Heaven had ordained;
sentences.n: 天命 'the decree of Heaven' is the Zhou idea that Heaven 天 confers a charge 命 — on a dynasty, and here on a person. Zhu Xi makes it the working of the heavenly Way in all things, 'the reason things are as they ought to be' (事物所以當然之故): at forty he saw what each thing ought to be; at fifty he knew why.

sentences.t: 六十而耳順，
sentences.l: at sixty, the ear compliant;
sentences.i: at sixty what I heard went in without resistance;
sentences.n: 耳順 'the ear compliant' is the most puzzling stage. Zhu Xi: 聲入心通 'sounds entered and the heart understood' — whatever he heard, he grasped at once without having to think it through. Master Cheng puts it shortly: 'all that he heard got through'.

sentences.t:
七十而從心所欲，
不踰矩。」

morph.gloss: the square — the carpenter's square, the standard

sentences.l:
at seventy, following what the heart wanted,
not overstepping the square.”
sentences.i: at seventy I could go where my heart wished and never stray beyond the carpenter's square.”
sentences.n: 從 is cóng 'to follow' (Zhu Xi: 從如字, the ordinary reading; 從 also stands for 縱 zòng 'to give rein to', and He Yan's text writes 縱). 心所欲 is 'what the heart wanted': 所 turns 欲 'to want' into 'that which (it) wanted'. 矩 is the carpenter's square, the tool that makes corners true; Zhu Xi glosses it 法度之器. The point is that desire and rule have become one. Master Cheng says the sage may not have needed these stages himself and set them out as a pattern for learners; Zhu Xi adds that it was no mock modesty — the sage did feel his own progress, though others could not see it.

sentences.t:
孟懿子問孝。
子曰：「無違。」

morph.gloss: Meng Yizi — a grandee of Lu

sentences.l:
Meng Yizi asked about filial devotion.
The Master said: “Never go against.”
sentences.i: Meng Yizi asked about being a good son. The Master said: “Do not go against.”
sentences.n: 孟懿子 is Zhongsun Heji 仲孫何忌, head of the Meng (Zhongsun) house, one of the three great families that held real power in Lu. The answer is two characters, and deliberately so: 無違 'no going against', with no object. Go against what? Zhu Xi says 'against principle' (不背於理), and the next unit shows why Confucius left it open.

sentences.t:
樊遲御，
子告之曰：「
孟孫問孝於我，
我對曰：『無違。』」

morph.gloss: Fan Chi — the disciple Fan Xu
Chi, from Fan Xu's courtesy name 子遲
Mengsun — Meng Yizi, by his clan name
Meng, the clan name (Mengsun, Zhongsun) of Lu
Sun, 'grandson', the clan name's last part (孟孫, 季孫, 仲孫)

sentences.i: When Fan Chi was driving the Master's chariot, the Master told him: “Mengsun asked me what it is to be a good son, and I told him, ‘Do not go against.’”
sentences.n: 樊遲 Fan Chi is Fan Xu 樊須, a younger disciple; 御 is to drive a chariot, here the Master's. 孟孫 is the same Meng Yizi, now called by his clan. 對 is the word for answering a superior. Zhu Xi explains the scene: Yizi had not understood and did not ask again, and Confucius feared he would take 'not going against' to mean obeying his parents' every order, so he raised it with Fan Chi, to bring the point out.

sentences.t:
樊遲曰：「何謂也？」
子曰：「
生，事之以禮；
死，葬之以禮，
祭之以禮。」

morph.gloss: Chi, from Fan Xu's courtesy name 子遲

sentences.l:
Fan Chi said: “What does it mean?”
The Master said: “Alive, serve them by the rites;
dead, bury them by the rites,
sacrifice to them by the rites.”
sentences.i: Fan Chi said: “What did you mean?” The Master said: “While they live, serve them as the rites require; when they die, bury them as the rites require, and offer sacrifice to them as the rites require.”
sentences.n: 何謂也 'what (is it) called?' is the standard way to ask 'what do you mean?' The answer reveals the missing object of 無違: not 'never go against your parents' but 'never go against the rites'. 生 and 死 stand alone as time clauses, 'living… dead…'. Zhu Xi points out the sting: the three great families of Lu, Meng Yizi's among them, used rites above their station, and this was a warning — put so that it did not seem aimed at them alone.

sentences.t:
孟武伯問孝。
子曰：「父母
唯其疾之憂。」
sentences.l:
Meng Wubo asked about filial devotion.
The Master said: “Father and mother —
only over his illness do they worry.”
sentences.i: Meng Wubo asked about being a good son. The Master said: “Your father and mother have one worry above all: that you may fall ill.”
sentences.n: 孟武伯 is Zhongsun Zhi 仲孫彘, son of the Meng Yizi of 2.5. 唯…之… is a pattern to learn: the object is fronted and marked by 之, with 唯 'only' in front — 唯其疾之憂 'only his illness, (that) they worry over'. Zhu Xi reads it this way: parents' love is so complete that they fear only that their child may fall ill, and a son who takes that to heart will look after himself and keep out of trouble. He records an older reading too: a son should give his parents nothing to worry over except illness, which no one can help — never his wrongdoing.

sentences.t:
子游問孝。
子曰：「今之孝者，
是謂能養。
至於犬馬，
皆能有養；
不敬，
何以别乎？」

morph.gloss: the Master (alone as speaker, always Confucius)
You, in Ziyou's name (言偃, courtesy name 子游)

sentences.l:
Ziyou asked about filial devotion.
The Master said: “Today's filial ones —
this means being able to feed (parents).
Coming to dogs and horses,
all can be fed;
not reverent,
by what is it distinguished?”
sentences.i: Ziyou asked about being a good son. The Master said: “What passes for a good son these days means one who can keep his parents fed. But dogs and horses are all kept fed too. Without reverence, what is there to tell the two apart?”
sentences.n: 子游 Ziyou is Yan Yan 言偃, a disciple known for his learning in the rites. 今之孝者 'the filial of today': 者 makes 孝 a noun, 'those who count as filial'. 養 is to feed and provide for (Zhu Xi: 飲食供奉); he marks it 去聲, the old reading yàng for supporting one's elders, which modern practice does not keep: we give yǎng. The 'dogs and horses' line can be read two ways. Zhu Xi: people feed their dogs and horses too, so if your care for your parents lacks reverence, how is it different from keeping animals? An older reading has dogs and horses as the ones who serve and support men. 何以别乎 'by what distinguish?' — 以 'by' with its object fronted as 何 'what'. 别 is printed in this form in the edition; it is the word 別 bié.

sentences.t:
子夏問孝。
子曰：「色難。
有事，弟子服其勞；
有酒食，先生饌：
曾是以為孝乎？」

morph.gloss: the Master (alone as speaker, always Confucius)
food — Zhu Xi reads sì 'cooked grain'
the elders — fathers and elder brothers

sentences.l:
Zixia asked about filial devotion.
The Master said: “The countenance is hard.
There is work — the young take on its toil;
there is wine and food — the elders are served:
is this ever taken as filial devotion?”
sentences.i: Zixia asked about being a good son. The Master said: “The hard part is the look on your face. When there is work to be done, the young take the labour on themselves; when there is wine and food, it goes to their elders — but can that alone be counted as being a good son?”
sentences.n: 色難 'the countenance is hard': two characters, a whole teaching. Zhu Xi explains that deep love shows itself as warmth, warmth as a glad face, a glad face as gentleness — and that is the hard thing; running errands and serving meals are not enough. An older reading he records: 'what is hard is reading your parents' faces and going along with them'. 弟子 here is 'the young' as in 1.6, and 先生 'those born first', the elders (Zhu Xi: 父兄 'fathers and elder brothers') — not yet 'teacher' or 'Mr'. 食 Zhu Xi reads sì, 'cooked grain, a meal'; modern practice reads shí. 曾 is céng, 'ever' (Zhu Xi: 曾猶嘗也); others read zēng, 'after all, can it be that'. 以為 'to take as': 是以為孝 'is this taken as filial?' The four answers on filial devotion (2.5–2.8), Master Cheng says, each fit the man who asked.

sentences.t:
子曰：「
吾與回言終日，
不違，如愚。
退而省其私，
亦足以發。
回也不愚。」
sentences.l:
The Master said: “I talk with Hui the whole day:
he does not object — as if slow.
He withdraws, and I look into his private life:
it, too, is quite enough to bring (it) out.
Hui is not slow.”
sentences.i: The Master said: “I can talk with Hui all day long and he never raises an objection, as though he were dull. But when he has gone and I look at how he lives on his own, I find he brings to light all that I said. Hui is anything but dull.”
sentences.n: 回 Hui is Yan Hui 顏回 (courtesy name Ziyuan 子淵), the disciple Confucius loved most, who died young. As with Ci in 1.15, the Master calls him by his personal name. 不違 here is not 'not disobey' but 'not differ': he takes in everything and asks nothing (Zhu Xi: 有聽受而無問難). 私 is his private life — Zhu Xi: when he is at leisure on his own, not when he comes to ask. 發 is to bring out into the open: what he does lights up the Master's teaching. The ending 回也不愚 turns the 如愚 'as if slow' of the first half inside out.

sentences.t:
子曰：「
視其所以，
sentences.l: The Master said: “Look at what he does;
sentences.i: The Master said: “Watch what a man does;
sentences.n: Three verbs of seeing climb in this passage — 視 'look at', 觀 'observe', 察 'examine' — and Zhu Xi says each is more searching than the last. 所以 is 所 'that which' + 以, which Zhu Xi glosses as 為 'to do': 'that which he does'. Do good, he says, and you are a gentleman; do ill and you are a small man.

sentences.t: 觀其所由，
sentences.l: observe what he goes by;
sentences.i: look into what moves him to it;
sentences.n: 由 is 'to follow, to go by': Zhu Xi takes it as the source of the act, the intent behind it. A deed may be good, he says, while the purpose it comes from is not. He records another reading: 由 = 行 'to go', 'the way he goes about it'.

sentences.t: 察其所安。

morph.gloss: (he) is at ease in, rests content in

sentences.l: examine what he rests content in.
sentences.i: find out what he is content with.
sentences.n: 安 'to be at ease in' is the deepest test: Zhu Xi says it is what the heart takes pleasure in. If a man acts rightly and his motives are right but his heart does not delight in it, it will not last.

sentences.t:
人焉廋哉！
人焉廋哉！」
sentences.l:
Where can a man hide?
Where can a man hide?”
sentences.i: How can anyone keep himself hidden? How can anyone keep himself hidden?”
sentences.n: 焉 here is a question word, 'how? where?' (Zhu Xi: 焉何也), not the fused 於之 'at it' you met in 1.14. 廋 sōu is a rare word, 'to hide' (Zhu Xi: 匿也). 哉 is a particle of exclamation. Zhu Xi on the repetition: 'he says it twice to make it plain'.

sentences.t:
子曰：「
溫故而知新，
可以為師矣。」

morph.gloss: the old — what one learned before

sentences.l:
The Master said: “Going back over the old and knowing the new —
one can thereby be a teacher.”
sentences.i: The Master said: “A man who goes back over what he learned before and each time finds something new in it can serve others as a teacher.”
sentences.n: 溫 is 'warm', and so 'to warm up again, to go back over': Zhu Xi glosses it 尋繹 'to follow out a thread'. 故 is 'the old' — what one heard before — and 新 'the new', what one now gains from it. 可以 'can thereby'. Zhu Xi sets this against mere memorized learning, which has a fixed store and soon runs out; real learning keeps answering.

sentences.t: 子曰：「君子不器。」

morph.gloss: the Master (alone as speaker, always Confucius)

sentences.l: The Master said: “The gentleman — not a vessel.”
sentences.i: The Master said: “A gentleman is not a tool made for one use.”
sentences.n: 器 is any made thing with a single function — a cup, a pot, a tool. Classical Chinese often needs no verb 'to be': 君子不器 is just 'gentleman not vessel'. Zhu Xi: each vessel fits its own use and cannot serve another; a man of full virtue lacks nothing, so his usefulness reaches everywhere — he is not merely one talent or one skill.

sentences.t:
子貢問君子。
子曰：「先行其言，
而後從之。」

morph.gloss: the Master (alone as speaker, always Confucius)
the Master (alone as speaker, always Confucius)

sentences.l:
Zigong asked about the gentleman.
The Master said: “First he puts his words into practice,
and afterward (they) follow it.”
sentences.i: Zigong asked about the gentleman. The Master said: “He acts on what he would say before he says it, and lets his words follow the deed.”
sentences.n: The sentence is spare and can be cut two ways. Zhu Xi, quoting Zhou Fuxian, reads it whole: he does what he would say before saying it, and says it after it is done — 先 'first' and 後 'after' are a pair. Others stop after 先行: 'he acts first; his words follow after'. Fan Zuyu adds why this was said to Zigong: his trouble was not speaking but doing — he was the eloquent one.

sentences.t:
子曰：「
君子周而不比；
小人比而不周。」

morph.gloss: the Master (alone as speaker, always Confucius)
the small man — the petty man, the gentleman's opposite

sentences.l:
The Master said: “The gentleman is all-round and not partisan;
the small man partisan and not all-round.”
sentences.i: The Master said: “The gentleman is open to everyone and does not form cliques; the small man forms cliques and is open to no one.”
sentences.n: 小人 'the small man' is the 君子's opposite, and you will meet the pair constantly; Zhu Xi says they differ 'like dark and light, night and day'. Both 周 and 比 mean being close to people. 周 is all-round (Zhu Xi: 普徧 'universal'), 比 is one-sided (偏黨 'partisan'); the difference is between public-minded and private. Zhu Xi reads 比 bì, the old reading for 'to band together'; modern practice reads bǐ. Notice how 而不 joins the clauses: 'A, and not B', then reversed for the small man.

sentences.t:
子曰：「
學而不思則罔，
思而不學則殆。」

morph.gloss: in the dark, at a loss

sentences.l:
The Master said: “Learning and not thinking — then in the dark;
thinking and not learning — then in danger.”
sentences.i: The Master said: “Study without reflection leaves you groping; reflection without study puts you at risk.”
sentences.n: Two lines that mirror each other, joined by 則 'then' as in 1.6. 學 here is learning from what others teach and do; 思 is thinking it through for oneself. Zhu Xi glosses: without seeking it in your own mind, you are 'in the dark and gain nothing' (罔); without practising the thing itself, you are 'at risk and not at ease' (殆).

sentences.t:
子曰：「
攻乎異端，
斯害也已。」

morph.gloss: to work at, devote oneself to
other teachings — doctrines from a different end

sentences.l:
The Master said: “Working at teachings from another end —
this is harm indeed.”
sentences.i: The Master said: “To give yourself to doctrines that are not the Way brings only harm.”
sentences.n: 攻 is first 'to attack', and also 'to work at' (as craftsmen work jade). Zhu Xi, following Fan Zuyu, takes the second: 'to work at exclusively'. 異端 is 'different ends' — teachings other than the sages'. Fan Zuyu, quoted by Zhu Xi, names the schools of Yang Zhu and Mo Di, which came after Confucius' day, and his Cheng masters add Buddhism, 'nearer to the truth, and so more harmful'. 也已 is a doubled final particle, strong assertion. Another reading takes 攻 as 'attack' and 已 as 'to stop': 'attack strange doctrines, and the harm ends'. He Yan's text has 也已矣, the same sense.

sentences.t:
子曰：「由！
誨女知之乎？
知之為知之，
不知為不知，
是知也。」
sentences.l:
The Master said: “Yóu!
Shall I teach you knowing it?
Knowing it, count it as knowing it;
not knowing, count it as not knowing —
this is knowing.”
sentences.i: The Master said: “Yóu, shall I teach you about knowing? When you know a thing, treat it as known; when you do not, treat it as not known. That is what knowing is.”
sentences.n: 由 Yóu is Zhong You 仲由, courtesy name Zilu 子路, the bold and impulsive disciple. The Master calls him by his personal name, which we write Yóu to keep it apart from English 'you'. Zhu Xi says he was 'fond of courage', and liable to pass off what he did not know as known. 女 here is read rǔ, 'you' (= 汝; Zhu Xi: 女音汝), not nǚ 'woman' — learn it now, it recurs. 知之 'know it' turns on itself: 為 is 'to count as'. Zhu Xi reads the last 知 as 'knowing' too: even if you cannot know everything, there is no self-deception, and it still counts as knowing (不害其為知) — and from there more can be known. Many modern readers take it as zhì, the word later written 智 'wisdom'.

sentences.t: 子張學干禄。

morph.gloss: the Master (alone as speaker, always Confucius)

sentences.l: Zizhang was learning to seek a salary.
sentences.i: Zizhang was studying with an eye to an official salary.
sentences.n: 子張 Zizhang is Zhuansun Shi 顓孫師, a younger disciple. 干 is 'to seek' (Zhu Xi: 求也), 禄 an officer's pay, the stipend of office — the character is printed 禄 in this edition, the word 祿 lù. So 學干禄 is learning how to get a post: Zhu Xi treats it as a fault, which the answer corrects.

sentences.t:
子曰：「
多聞，闕疑，
慎言其餘，則寡尤；
多見，闕殆，
慎行其餘，則寡悔。
言寡尤，行寡悔，
禄在其中矣。」
sentences.l:
The Master said: “Hear much, leave aside what is doubtful,
carefully speak the rest — then few faults;
see much, leave aside what is unsafe,
carefully act on the rest — then few regrets.
In speech few faults, in conduct few regrets:
the salary is there within it.”
sentences.i: The Master said: “Listen widely, set aside what you are unsure of, and speak with care about the rest, and you will seldom be at fault. Look widely, set aside what seems unsafe, and act with care on the rest, and you will seldom have cause to regret. Seldom at fault in what you say, seldom regretting what you do — the salary will come of itself.”
sentences.n: The two halves are built alike: 多 'much' + a verb of learning, 闕 'to leave a gap' — read quē, 'to leave out' — + what to leave, 慎 'careful' + speech or action, then the result with 則 'then'. Master Cheng's distinction, quoted by Zhu Xi: 尤 is blame that comes from outside, 悔 regret that comes from within. In 行寡悔 Zhu Xi reads 行 xìng, 'conduct', the noun; modern practice reads xíng throughout. 在其中 'is in the midst of it' is his point: the salary is not pursued, it arrives on its own. 見 is jiàn 'to see', not xiàn 'to appear'.

sentences.t:
哀公問曰：「
何為則民服？」
孔子對曰：「
舉直錯諸枉，則民服；
舉枉錯諸直，則民不服。」

morph.gloss: Duke Ai — the ruler of Lu
the many — Zhu Xi: 衆也

sentences.l:
Duke Ai asked, saying: “Doing what, then will the people submit?”
Kongzi answered, saying:
“Raise the straight, set aside the many crooked — then the people submit;
raise the crooked, set aside the many straight — then the people do not submit.”
sentences.i: Duke Ai asked: “What should I do to win the people's acceptance?” Confucius replied: “Raise up the upright and set aside all the crooked, and the people will accept you. Raise up the crooked and set aside all the upright, and they will not.”
sentences.n: 哀公 is Duke Ai of Lu (r. 494–468 BC), Confucius' ruler in his last years. Notice the speaker's name changes: when a ruler asks, the book writes 孔子對曰 'Kongzi answered', with the formal 對 — Zhu Xi says this honours the ruler. 孔子 Kongzi, 'Master Kong', is the name the West latinized as Confucius. 錯 is 'to set aside, to put away' (Zhu Xi: 捨置). 諸 Zhu Xi glosses as 衆 'the many'; others take it as the fused 之於 of 1.15: 'raise the straight and place them over the crooked'. Both make sense; we follow Zhu Xi. 直 and 枉 are 'straight' and 'bent', as of timber, and as of men.

sentences.t:
季康子問：「
使民敬，忠以勸，
如之何？」
子曰：「
臨之以莊，則敬；
孝慈，則忠；
舉善而敎不能，則勸。」

morph.gloss: Ji Kangzi — chief minister of Lu

sentences.i: Ji Kangzi asked: “How can I make the people reverent, give themselves wholly, and be spurred on to do well?” The Master said: “Approach them with dignity, and they will be reverent. Be a good son to your parents and kind to all, and they will give themselves to you wholly. Promote the good and teach those who fall short, and they will be spurred on.”
sentences.n: 季康子 is Jisun Fei 季孫肥, head of the Ji (Jisun) house, the most powerful of the three families and the real ruler of Lu. 如之何 is a fixed question: 'how does one deal with it?' The answer turns each of his three wishes back on him, with 則 'then' each time: the people's reverence, wholeheartedness and zeal follow from what he does himself. Zhu Xi: 莊 is a grave, upright bearing; 孝 toward his own parents and 慈 'kind' toward the people; 忠 is their being wholehearted toward him. Zhang Shi adds that these are things to do because they are right, not tricks to make the people so. 敎 is the edition's form of 教 jiào 'to teach'. He Yan's text reads 則民勸, 'then the people are encouraged'.

sentences.t:
或謂孔子曰：「
子奚不為政？」

morph.gloss: the Master (alone as speaker, always Confucius)

sentences.l: Someone said to Kongzi: “Why, sir, do you not take part in government?”
sentences.i: Someone said to Confucius: “Why are you not in government, sir?”
sentences.n: 或 is 'someone', an unnamed person. 子 here is not 'the Master' but the respectful 'you, sir' addressed to him. 奚 is a question word, 'why?' Zhu Xi dates the exchange to the first years of Duke Ding (509 BC on), when Confucius held no office.

sentences.t:
子曰：「《書》云：『孝乎！
惟孝，友于兄弟，
施於有政。』
是亦為政，
奚其為為政？」
sentences.l:
The Master said: “The Documents say:
‘Filial! Only filial, a friend to brothers,
extending it to the governing (of his house).’
This too is conducting government;
why must (only office) count as conducting government?”
sentences.i: The Master said: “The Documents say: ‘Filial, truly filial, and a friend to his brothers, he carried it over into the governing of his house.’ That too is taking part in government. Why should only holding office count as taking part?”
sentences.n: 《書》 is the Book of Documents, a collection of early speeches and royal pronouncements; Zhu Xi locates the quotation in its 君陳 chapter. He reads 孝乎 as the Documents' own exclamation on filial devotion, and 友 as being good to one's brothers (善兄弟曰友). 施於有政 he takes as extending this to the government of one's own household (一家之政) — which is why Confucius can say it too is government. 有政 is 'government': 有 before a noun is an old prefix with no meaning of its own, as in 有夏 'the Xia'. The last line has 為 twice: the first is 'count as', the second 'conduct' — 'why count (only office) as conducting government?' Zhu Xi adds that Confucius had reasons for staying out of office that could not be told to this questioner, so he answered with a truth that would do.

sentences.t:
子曰：「
人而無信，不知其可也。
大車無輗，
小車無軏，
其何以行之哉？」
sentences.l:
The Master said: “A man and yet without good faith —
I do not know what he can do.
A big cart without its crossbar,
a small carriage without its yoke-hook —
how would it go?”
sentences.i: The Master said: “I cannot see what use a man is if his word is not good. An ox-cart with no crossbar to the yoke, a carriage with no hook to the pole — how could either one go?”
sentences.n: 人而無信: 而 between a subject and its predicate gives 'a man, and yet without good faith' — in effect 'if a man…'. 不知其可 'I do not know his possible', what he could be good for. Zhu Xi explains the two parts: the 輗 ní is the crossbar at the end of an ox-cart's shafts, to which the yoke is tied; the 軏 yuè is the upturned hook at the end of a horse-carriage's pole, which holds the crossbar. Small pieces, but without them nothing is joined to what pulls it, and the vehicle cannot move. 何以…哉 'by what…!' is a rhetorical question.

sentences.t:
子張問：「
十世可知也？」

morph.gloss: the Master (alone as speaker, always Confucius)
(question — Zhu Xi notes one text has 乎)

sentences.l: Zizhang asked: “Ten ages hence — can they be known?”
sentences.i: Zizhang asked: “Can we know what will happen ten ages from now?”
sentences.n: 世 is usually 'a generation', thirty years. Zhu Xi takes it larger: one 世 is each time a new royal house changes the surname and receives the mandate — so 十世 is ten dynasties. 也 normally asserts; here it closes a question, and Zhu Xi quotes Lu Deming that one text reads 乎, the ordinary question particle.

sentences.t:
子曰：「
殷因於夏禮，
所損益可知也；
周因於殷禮，
所損益可知也；
其或繼周者，
雖百世可知也。」
sentences.i: The Master said: “The Yin took over the rites of the Xia, and we can know what it dropped and what it added. The Zhou took over the rites of the Yin, and we can know what it dropped and what it added. Whoever may succeed the Zhou, even a hundred ages from now, can be known in the same way.”
sentences.n: The three dynasties: Xia 夏, Yin 殷 (the Shang), and Zhou 周, under which Confucius lived. 因 is 'to rely on, to take over' (as in 1.13). 所損益 is 所 + two verbs: 'what (it) reduced and increased'. Zhu Xi, after Ma Rong, says what was carried over are the Three Bonds (ruler–minister, father–son, husband–wife) and Five Constants (humaneness, what is right, the rites, wisdom, good faith), which no dynasty can change; what was altered is only the outward detail — the balance of ornament and plainness, and the calendar. So the future can be known, not by divination but by seeing what lasts. He Yan's text reads 雖百世亦可知, 'even a hundred ages on, it too can be known'.

sentences.t:
子曰：「
非其鬼而祭之，諂也。

morph.gloss: spirit — of the dead, an ancestor

sentences.l:
The Master said: “Not one's own spirit, and yet sacrificing to it —
that is fawning.
sentences.i: The Master said: “To make offerings to spirits that are not yours to honour is to curry favour.
sentences.n: 鬼 here is the spirit of a dead person, an ancestor; Zhu Xi: 'spirits to whom it is not one's place to sacrifice'. Each family sacrificed to its own; offerings to others' are bids for blessing. 諂 is the fawning of 1.15, now aimed at the dead. 非…而… 'not…, and yet…' sets the wrong up in one clause.

sentences.t:
見義不為，
無勇也。」
sentences.l:
Seeing what is right and not doing it —
that is lacking courage.”
sentences.i: To see what is right and not act on it is to lack courage.”
sentences.n: The book ends on 義 'what is right' and 勇 'courage'. Zhu Xi: 知而不為 'to know it and not do it' — that is to lack courage. 見 is jiàn 'to see', 為 wéi 'to do'.
